**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — Coalition forces on Monday formally transferred security control of Iraq’s Anbar province—once the epicenter of the country’s Sunni insurgency—to Iraqi authorities. 

Although U.S. troops, who were patrolling Ramadi’s markets as recently as earlier this year, will remain stationed in the vast western province to assist local forces, their primary role will shift to a supporting capacity when needed.

President George W. Bush characterized the handover as a decisive victory against the al-Qaeda extremists who once dominated the region. "Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda—it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar," Bush declared in a statement.

Long a stronghold for Sunni insurgents and the site of frequent attacks on U.S.-led forces, Anbar has transformed into a center of tribal resistance against extremism. However, the province has also become the backdrop for an internal Sunni political struggle between the Iraqi Islamic Party—one of the nation's principal Sunni political factions—and the Awakening movement, Iraq's pioneer anti-al-Qaeda coalition.

More than 25,000 U.S. troops, predominantly Marines, serve in the sprawling province west of Baghdad. While they will remain deployed in the region for the time being, their mission will pivot to overwatch and Iraqi force assistance.

Brigadier General David Perkins, spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq, described the transition as a milestone for the entire nation. The formal ceremony took place in Ramadi, the provincial capital, attended by key Iraqi dignitaries and senior U.S. military leadership. 

"We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago," Perkins remarked. "And the fact that that has been able to be turned around, that the Iraqi citizens that live there want to stand up on their own, [that] they want to take control of the province on their own ... it's major progress not only for Anbar, but for all of Iraq."

Anbar is the eleventh of Iraq's eighteen provinces to revert to local security control, and notably the first Sunni-majority region to do so. The transition occurs amid a significant reduction in violence nationwide and growing calls from Iraqi officials for the United States to establish a firm timeline for troop withdrawal. 

The other provinces that have previously transitioned to Iraqi security control are Duhuk, Irbil, and Sulaimaniya in the northern Kurdish region, along with Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan in the Shiite-dominated south.

*CNN's Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon in Baghdad contributed to this report.*

# Coalition Forces Transfer Security Control of Anbar Province to Local Iraqi Command

In a significant milestone for the stabilization of Iraq, Coalition forces have formally handed over security control of Anbar province to local Iraqi forces. This transition marks a critical juncture in the nation’s path toward self-governance, as Anbar becomes the first Sunni-dominated province—and the eleventh out of Iraq’s eighteen provinces overall—to be returned to local security control.

The handover is particularly symbolic given the region's turbulent history. Once widely regarded as one of the most dangerous operational areas in Iraq, Anbar was formerly a central hub for the Sunni insurgency and a hotbed for militant violence. Over time, however, the security landscape shifted dramatically. Driven by local tribal alliances that rejected extremist violence, the province transformed from an insurgent stronghold into a vital bastion of anti-al-Qaeda opposition.

U.S. leadership hailed the transfer as a major turning point in the conflict. President George W. Bush and military spokesmen declared the handover a decisive victory against al-Qaeda extremists, who had previously sought to establish a permanent foothold in the region. 

While Iraqi forces now take the lead in day-to-day operations and regional security, Coalition involvement is far from over. More than 25,000 U.S. troops will remain stationed in Anbar to provide tactical support, training, and operational assistance to Iraqi forces as needed, ensuring that the progress made in the province remains secure.

**Historic Shift: Coalition Forces Hand Over Anbar Province Security to Iraqi Control**

In a pivotal moment for the future of Iraq, Coalition troops have formally transferred primary security responsibility for Anbar province over to Iraqi military and police forces. Once the bloody heartland of the Sunni insurgency and the deadliest stronghold for al-Qaeda in Iraq, the vast western province now enters a new phase of local governance. As local forces take the lead on the ground, remaining U.S. troops are stepping back into a supportive role focused on training, strategic advice, and logistical assistance.

### From Battleground to Turning Point

The significance of this transfer cannot be overstated given Anbar’s grim history during the conflict. Covering nearly a third of Iraq’s landmass and stretching from the outskirts of Baghdad to the Syrian border, the province was for years considered an untamable battleground. Cities like Fallujah and Ramadi became synonymous with intense urban warfare, where Coalition troops fought some of their fiercest combat actions in modern history. 

During the height of the violence, al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI) established a brutal grip over the local population, utilizing the region’s porous borders and rugged terrain as a staging ground for devastating attacks across the nation. 

The dramatic turnaround began in late 2006 with the emergence of the "Anbar Awakening" (also known as the *Sahwa*). Weary of al-Qaeda’s extreme violence, heavy-handed rule, and disruption of local life, prominent Sunni tribal leaders made the strategic decision to align themselves with U.S. forces. This local uprising, combined with the 2007 U.S. military troop surge, dramatically altered the security landscape. Thousands of local Sunnis joined official security forces and local guard units, systematically driving extremists out of the cities and towns they had terrorized for years.

### A Milestone for National Sovereignty

The formal transition ceremony took place in the provincial capital of Ramadi, attended by senior Iraqi government officials, military commanders, and local tribal leaders who had played a crucial role in defeating the insurgency. 

Anbar marks the eleventh of Iraq’s 18 provinces to be returned to Provincial Iraqi Control (PIC). Crucially, however, it represents the very first handover in a Sunni-dominated region. Previous transfers had been restricted largely to the relatively stable Kurdish north and the Shiite-majority provinces in the south. Reaching this milestone in a Sunni heartland offers a powerful demonstration of the central government’s expanding reach and growing institutional capacity.

Under the terms of the handover, Iraqi provincial police and army units will now handle day-to-day security operations, man checkpoints, and conduct counter-terrorism patrols. U.S. forces will remain staged at nearby bases, ready to provide quick-reaction support, intelligence sharing, and air assistance only if requested by Iraqi authorities.

### Looking Ahead

Military leaders and political analysts alike have hailed the transition as a crushing blow to al-Qaeda’s narrative, proving that local populations and national forces can successfully reclaim territories once thought lost to radical extremism. 

While significant political challenges remain—including economic reconstruction, tribal integration, and long-term reconciliation between political factions—the security handover in Anbar stands as a landmark victory. It underscores measurable progress in stabilizing the country and marks an essential step toward full Iraqi sovereignty and self-reliance.

**Title:** Echoes from the Tigris: How CNN and Baghdad Reshaped Global Journalism

For centuries, Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, was celebrated as a jewel of Islamic culture and a historic cradle of civilization. However, in the late 20th century, the global perception of this ancient city shifted dramatically—largely through the lens of a single news network: CNN.

The relationship between CNN and Iraq reached a defining milestone in January 1991 during the outbreak of the Gulf War. As Operation Desert Storm commenced, CNN correspondents Bernard Shaw, Peter Arnett, and John Holliman broadcast live from their room in the Al-Rashid Hotel in Baghdad. As anti-aircraft tracer fire lit up the night sky, millions of viewers around the world watched the reality of modern warfare unfold in real-time for the very first time. 

The famous phrase "Live from Baghdad" was not just a television cue; it was a watershed moment in media history. CNN’s groundbreaking coverage of the bombing of Baghdad transformed 24-hour cable news from a novel concept into an essential global utility.

Over a decade later, during the 2003 invasion of Iraq and the years of conflict that followed, CNN once again served as a major window into the region. From the fall of Saddam Hussein’s statue in Baghdad's Firdos Square to the complex narratives of reconstruction, political upheaval, and human resilience, the network's correspondents remained on the ground to document the nation's turbulent path.

Today, as Baghdad works to revitalize its historic streets, restore its cultural life, and build a stable future for Iraq, the city continues to draw international focus. The enduring connection between Baghdad, Iraq, and CNN remains a masterclass in war reporting, proving how journalism can bridge the distance between a localized conflict and a watching world.

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* U.S. military formally transfers security control of Anbar province to Iraqi forces.
* Once the deadliest region for American troops, Anbar was the epicenter of the Sunni insurgency.
* Transfer marks the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to return to Provincial Iraqi Control.
* Officials hail the move as a historic milestone, though security challenges remain.

---

**RAMADI, Iraq (CNN)** — In a dramatic symbol of changing tides in the Iraq War, the U.S. military on Monday officially handed over security responsibility for Anbar province—once the most violent and dangerous battleground in the country—to local Iraqi forces.

During a formal ceremony under tight security in the provincial capital of Ramadi, U.S. military commanders and Iraqi officials signed documents returning the vast desert region to Provincial Iraqi Control (PIC). 

The transfer marks a stunning turnaround for a region that was once written off by top U.S. military strategists as a lost cause.

"Today is a triumph for the people of Anbar, and a profound step forward for all of Iraq," said Maj. Gen. John Kelly, the top U.S. Marine commander in western Iraq, addressing a crowd of tribal leaders, local police chiefs, and Iraqi politicians. "Where violence and fear once ruled these streets, law and order now stand."

Anbar is the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to be returned to Iraqi control, but military analysts consider this handover the most significant to date. 

### From 'Crucible of Violence' to Relative Calm

Sprawling across Iraq's western border with Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, the Sunni-dominated province was for years the beating heart of the anti-U.S. insurgency and the operational hub for Al Qaeda in Iraq (AQI). 

It was the bloody backdrop for some of the fiercest fighting of the war, including the twin battles for Fallujah in 2004 and years of deadly urban warfare in Ramadi. Nearly 1,300 American service members lost their lives in Anbar—more than in any other Iraqi province.

The turning point came in late 2006 with the rise of the "Anbar Awakening" (Sahwa), a movement in which local Sunni tribal leaders, fed up with Al Qaeda’s brutal tactics and strict religious imposition, allied themselves with U.S. forces. 

That alliance, coupled with the 2007 U.S. troop "surge," led to a dramatic drop in violence across the province.

"This day was paid for in the blood of Iraqi civilians, Iraqi security forces, and coalition troops," Anbar Governor Maamoun Sami Rasheed al-Alwani told reporters through a translator. "We have reclaimed our home from the terrorists, and we will not let them return."

### A Test for Local Forces

Under the terms of the transfer, Iraqi police and army units will now take the lead in daily security operations and checkpoint management throughout cities like Fallujah, Ramadi, and Haditha. 

U.S. Marines and Army soldiers will fall back to larger bases outside urban centers, stepping into a supporting role focused on logistics, training, and tactical advice. American forces will only re-enter the cities if explicitly requested by the provincial governor and authorized by Baghdad.

Despite the celebration, U.S. and Iraqi commanders expressed cautious optimism, acknowledging that major hurdles remain.

While insurgent attacks in Anbar have dropped by more than 90 percent over the past two years, Al Qaeda in Iraq retains the capability to launch devastating insurgent attacks, according to coalition intelligence reports.

"The threat has diminished, but it has not disappeared," CNN senior international correspondent Nic Robertson reported from Ramadi. "The real test for the Iraqi security forces will be maintaining this fragile peace without the daily, visible presence of American firepower."

Political friction also looms over the region. Tensions persist between the local Sunni leaders in Anbar and the Shiite-dominated central government in Baghdad over funding, police recruitment, and political representation ahead of upcoming provincial elections.

Still, for the residents of Ramadi, the sight of Iraqi police taking the lead in their streets brings a sense of long-awaited normalcy. 

"Years ago, we could not leave our homes without fear of bombs or bullets," said Ramadi resident Ahmed al-Dulaimi, watching the convoy of Iraqi police vehicles fly national flags through the city center. "Today, we see our own people protecting us. It is a new beginning."

counterfactuals.output:
**PRESS DISPATCH**  
**DATELINE:** BAGHDAD — Sept. 1, 2008  
**BYLINE:** Foreign Correspondent, Baghdad Bureau  

**HEADLINE: US Hands Control of Anbar to Iraqi Forces in Historic Ramadi Ceremony**

BAGHDAD — In a landmark moment for the war in Iraq, the U.S. military today formally transferred security responsibility of Anbar province—and its volatile capital, Ramadi—to Iraqi forces, marking a dramatic turnaround for a region that was once the bloodiest battleground of the insurgency. 

Anbar is the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to return to Provincial Iraqi Control (PIC), but the political and symbolic weight of today’s handover in Ramadi far outweighs those that came before it. Just two years ago, U.S. military intelligence reports declared the vast, Sunni-dominated western desert province virtually lost to Al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI). 

Today, Iraqi soldiers and police stood at attention alongside U.S. Marines in Ramadi, taking the lead in securing a city where burnt-out tanks and sniper alleyways have slowly given way to bustling market stalls and rebuilt police stations.

The catalyst for this pivotal shift was the emergence of the *Sahwa*, or the Sunni Awakening movement. Beginning in late 2006, local Sunni tribal leaders—weary of Al-Qaeda’s brutal tactics, strict religious mandates, and extrajudicial killings—decided to break ranks with foreign jihadists and ally themselves with U.S. forces. Armed and funded under the Awakening program, thousands of local Sunni fighters joined security volunteers, driving AQI out of their strongholds in Ramadi and Fallujah.

Speaking from Washington following the handover, President George W. Bush hailed the transfer as proof that the 2007 troop "surge" strategy had delivered tangible results.

"Anbar province was once written off as lost to Al-Qaeda," President Bush said in a statement released by the White House. "Today, thanks to the courage of the Iraqi people, our military, and the brave local leaders who stood up against tyranny, Anbar has been turned around. It is a striking demonstration of progress and proof that a peaceful, self-governing Iraq is attainable."

While Washington celebrated the milestone, military officials on the ground in Baghdad maintained a tone of cautious optimism, acknowledging that security in the province remains fragile. 

Major General David Perkins, the chief U.S. military spokesman in Baghdad, emphasized that while Iraqi forces are taking the lead, Coalition troops will remain in a supporting role to ensure the gains are not erased.

"The transfer of Anbar is a dramatic demonstration of how far the Iraqi security forces have come in terms of capability and readiness," Maj. Gen. Perkins told reporters during a briefing in the capital. "However, this is not an exit. It is a transition. The enemy in Anbar is down, but they are not completely out, and our forces will continue to advise, assist, and support our Iraqi partners as they maintain the security of their own sovereign territory."

Despite the official celebrations, anxiety simmers beneath the surface in Ramadi. Many leaders within the Sunni Awakening movement remain deeply suspicious of Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s Shia-dominated central government in Baghdad. Awakening commanders have voiced growing concerns over whether the Baghdad government will fulfill its promises to integrate *Sahwa* fighters into the official Iraqi army and civil service, or if old sectarian rivalries will resurface as U.S. troops step back.

For now, however, the streets of Ramadi belong to the Iraqi security forces. For a city that spent years as the epicenter of a bloody war, today brought a rare moment of pride, relief, and a tentative glimpse of a post-American future.

**U.S. Hands Over Control of Anbar, Marking Historic Shift in Former Sunni Insurgent Heartland**

**RAMADI, Iraq** — In a milestone moment for the security landscape of post-invasion Iraq, the United States military today officially transferred primary control of Anbar province to Iraqi security forces. 

The handover of the vast, western desert territory—once the deadliest battleground for American troops and the epicenter of the Sunni insurgency—is being hailed by coalition and Iraqi officials as a major turning point toward national self-reliance.

Anbar is the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to be returned to Provincial Iraqi Control (PIC), but its transfer carries unique political and symbolic weight: it is the very first Sunni-dominated province to be transitioned back to Iraqi authority. 

At a formal ceremony held in the provincial capital of Ramadi under heavy security, Iraqi commanders and provincial officials signed the transfer documents alongside senior U.S. military leaders. The Iraqi national flag was raised over government buildings that just two years ago were daily targets for mortar attacks and suicide bombers.

"This day is a victory for all Iraqis," declared Anbar Governor Maamoun Sami Rasheed during his address. "Anbar was once a dark land of terrorism, but today it returns to its rightful place as a beacon of security and unity."

### From Heartland of Insurgency to Turning Point

Covering roughly one-third of Iraq's landmass and stretching to the borders of Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, Anbar was for years considered a lost cause by many military strategists. Iconic cities such as Fallujah and Ramadi saw some of the fiercest combat of the war, including the bloody siege of Fallujah in late 2004. 

The province’s turnaround began in late 2006 with the rise of the "Anbar Awakening" (also known as the *Sahwa* movement), in which local Sunni tribal leaders joined forces with American troops to push out foreign fighters associated with Al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI). The success of the Awakening became the blueprint for security strategies used across the country during the 2007–2008 U.S. troop surge.

Lt. Gen. Lloyd Austin, the top day-to-day U.S. commander in Iraq, praised the resilience of the local population. "The people of Anbar chose peace over violence," Austin said at the ceremony. "Today's transfer is a testament to the sacrifice of Iraqi citizens, their security forces, and coalition troops."

### U.S. Troop Presence to Remain

While the handover marks a significant step back from direct American tactical command in the region, U.S. forces are far from leaving the province entirely. 

Approximately **28,000 U.S. troops**—primarily Marines and Army personnel—will remain stationed at major bases in Anbar, such as Al-Asad Airbase and Camp Fallujah. Their mission, however, will shift fundamentally from frontline combat operations to an advisory and support role. 

Under the new agreement, Iraqi police and army units will take the lead on routine patrols, city checkpoints, and counter-terrorism operations. U.S. troops will stay in the background, providing specialized assistance such as air support, intelligence sharing, logistics, and quick-reaction forces if local units find themselves overwhelmed.

### The Road to 11 Provinces

Prior to Anbar’s transfer, the ten provinces previously returned to Iraqi security control were concentrated heavily in the Shiite-majority south and the autonomous Kurdish north. 

The ten provinces previously transferred to Iraqi control are:

1. **Muthanna** (Transferred July 2006)
2. **Dhi Qar** (Transferred September 2006)
3. **Najaf** (Transferred December 2006)
4. **Maysan** (Transferred April 2007)
5. **Erbil** (Transferred May 2007 — Kurdistan Region)
6. **Sulaymaniyah** (Transferred May 2007 — Kurdistan Region)
7. **Dohuk** (Transferred May 2007 — Kurdistan Region)
8. **Karbala** (Transferred July 2007)
9. **Basra** (Transferred December 2007)
10. **Qadisiyah** (Transferred July 2008)

With Anbar becoming the 11th, coalition officials expressed confidence that the transfer would pave the way for other volatile, ethnically mixed provinces—including Babel, Diyala, and eventual handover of the capital, Baghdad—in the coming months.

### Fragile Progress

Despite the celebratory atmosphere in Ramadi, military officials caution that the security situation in Anbar remains fragile. Remnants of insurgent networks still attempt sporadic attacks, and political tensions between Anbar’s Sunni leaders and the Shiite-led central government in Baghdad continue to pose a long-term threat to stability.

Nevertheless, for the residents of Anbar and the U.S. military command, today's transition represents a unimaginable milestone compared to the province's darkest days.

"We have proved that security is possible when the people stand together," said Ramadi local police chief Maj. Gen. Tariq Youssef. "We are ready to protect our own cities."

**U.S. HANDS CONTROL OF ANBAR PROVINCE TO IRAQI FORCES IN HISTORIC TURNING POINT**

**DATELINE:** RAMADI, Iraq — September 1, 2008  
**By:** Steven R. Hurst  

In a milestone that would have seemed unthinkable just two years ago, the U.S. military on Monday formally transferred security control of Anbar province—once the deadliest battleground in Iraq and the heartland of the Sunni insurgency—to Iraqi government forces.

At a high-security ceremony in the provincial capital of Ramadi, U.S. Marine Maj. Gen. John Kelly signed documents handing over primary responsibility for the vast western desert region to Anbar Gov. Maamoon Sami Rasheed al-Alwani. 

The symbolic handover marks Anbar as the 11th of Iraq’s 18 provinces to return to provincial Iraqi control (PIC), and the first majority-Sunni territory to do so.

"Today is a day of victory for the people of Anbar," Gov. Alwani told a crowd of Iraqi officials, local sheiks, and coalition military commanders gathered under a heavy guard of Iraqi police and U.S. Marines. "The darkness of terrorism has been lifted, and a new era of security and reconstruction begins."

### FROM "POLITICALLY LOST" TO MODEL OF SUCCESS

The transfer represents a dramatic reversal of fortune for the U.S. campaign in Iraq. Sprawling across Iraq’s western border with Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, Anbar was long the epicenter of the bloody fight against U.S. troops, featuring brutal urban battles in Fallujah and Ramadi. 

As late as late 2006, a leaked U.S. Marine Corps intelligence report declared that Anbar was "politically lost" and that defeat was imminent, with Al-Qaeda in Iraq (AQI) exerting near-total control over the population through fear, public executions, and strict religious law.

However, the tide turned dramatically in late 2006 and 2007 with the rise of the *Sahwa*, or "Anbar Awakening." Disgusted by Al-Qaeda's extreme violence and economic dominance, local Sunni tribal leaders led by Sheikh Abdul Sattar Abu Risha allied with U.S. forces to turn their weapons against the foreign-led jihadists.

Combined with President George W. Bush’s "surge" of 30,000 additional U.S. troops, the Awakening successfully drove AQI out of the province's key cities.

"The people of Anbar decided they wanted peace," said Maj. Gen. Kelly during his address. "They turned against the murderers and the terrorists. Today, we honor the courage of the local sheiks, the police, and the Marines who gave their lives to make this moment possible."

### SYMBOLIC MILESTONE IN AN ELECTION YEAR

The handover comes at a critical juncture in Washington, where the Iraq War remains a central issue in the U.S. presidential campaign between Republican Sen. John McCain and Democratic Sen. Barack Obama. 

McCain’s campaign is expected to point to the Anbar transfer as definitive proof that the troop surge strategy championed by the Bush administration has succeeded. Conversely, Obama’s campaign has argued that the improvement in security validates his call for a phased withdrawal of American combat brigades to force Iraqi political reconciliation.

White House Press Secretary Dana Perino praised the transfer on Monday morning, calling it "a major step forward" while cautioning that "security conditions remain fragile."

### FRAGILE CALM AND REMAINING RISKS

Despite the celebratory tone in Ramadi, U.S. commanders acknowledge that Anbar remains far from completely peaceful. insurgent sleeper cells continue to carry out targeted assassinations and suicide attacks. Just hours before the ceremony, political tensions hung over the region following a series of minor bomb blasts elsewhere in the country over the weekend.

The ultimate test for Anbar will be political and economic integration. Long-standing friction remains between the Sunni tribal leaders in Anbar and the Shiite-led central government of Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki in Baghdad. 

A central point of concern is the future of the roughly 90,000 Sunni fighters known as the "Sons of Iraq"—many of them former insurgents—who are currently on the U.S. military payroll. The Maliki government has promised to slowly absorb a portion of these fighters into the official Iraqi army and police forces, but Sunnis remain deeply skeptical of Baghdad's commitment.

For now, American combat forces in Anbar will step back into a supporting role, moving into large outposts outside urban centers. They will remain available to provide air support, logistics, and quick-reaction forces if Iraqi troops find themselves overwhelmed.

"We are not leaving," Gen. Kelly assured local reporters after the signing ceremony. "We are simply stepping aside to let the rightful owners of Anbar take the lead."

***

*(AP Wire Reports and Pool Material contributed to this story.)*

**RAMADI, Iraq (CNN)** — In a milestone moment for the future of Anbar province, coalition forces officially handed over security control of Ramadi to Iraqi provincial authorities on Tuesday, marking a dramatic turnaround for a city once considered the most dangerous stronghold of the Sunni insurgency.

During a ceremony under tight security at the provincial headquarters, U.S. commanders signed over operational control to local Iraqi army and police units. The transition comes after years of heavy fighting in the provincial capital, where U.S. Marines and soldiers fought block-by-block battles against fighters linked to al Qaeda in Iraq.

The shift in Ramadi is widely seen as a key test for Iraq’s military capabilities as coalition forces gradually transition from a combat role to an advisory one across the country.

**Watch local Iraqi police march through the streets of Ramadi as coalition forces step back »**

Speaking through a translator at the ceremony, Anbar Gov. Maamoun Sami Rasheed praised the resilience of local citizens and the cooperation between local Sunni tribes and coalition troops, a movement known as the "Anbar Awakening." 

"This day belongs to the people of Ramadi who stood against terror and chose peace," Rasheed said. "Our forces are ready to protect our streets, our families, and our future."

At the peak of the violence between 2004 and 2006, Ramadi was virtually a war zone, with daily mortar attacks, roadside bombs, and sniper fire. The turning point came when local Sunni tribal leaders turned against foreign jihadists, forming local security councils that eventually integrated into the official Iraqi police force.

Despite the celebration, U.S. commanders urged cautious optimism, noting that while violence in the region has dropped significantly, insurgent sleeper cells still pose a threat. 

"The Iraqi forces have made extraordinary strides, but the work is not over," said Maj. Gen. Martin Smith, who oversees coalition operations in western Iraq. "We will remain nearby to provide support, logistics, and training, but the front line now belongs to Iraq."

U.S. troops will now reposition to bases outside the city center, remaining on standby to assist if requested by local officials. 

***

*CNN's Michael Holmes reported from Ramadi, and Arwa Damon contributed to this report from Baghdad. Written by Eric Fiegel in Atlanta.*
